title: Cueing Attention in Time... AKA the Three Benefits of a Good Check for Understanding good-check-for-understanding/
author: Mike Hobbiss
summary: Mike Hobbiss, building on his previous post about spatial attention cueing, argues that a well-designed check for understanding (CFU) delivers three distinct benefits, not just the one most commonly discussed. Beyond the well-known assessment-for-learning function - giving teachers diagnostic information about what students understand - he shows via 'interpolated testing' research that quizzing students partway through a lesson also functions as retrieval practice, measurably improving recall of the material already covered compared to a restudy control group. The more surprising third benefit, which Hobbiss frames as the article's central discovery, is that students who were quizzed on earlier material also performed better on a final test of content that came after the quiz - material both groups experienced identically - and reported less mind-wandering during that later content. He attributes this to 'test expectancy': once students believe information will be tested, their attention to subsequently-presented material sharpens, priming learning that hasn't happened yet. Hobbiss concludes that a CFU delivers all three benefits only if it is signposted to students in advance and requires them to actively retrieve information from memory, and closes candidly acknowledging that translating this into precise, non-distracting classroom cueing 'is not easy.'
points: Hobbiss identifies three distinct benefits of a well-designed check for understanding, beyond the commonly cited assessment-for-learning function: retrieval practice for prior material, and 'test expectancy' effects on material not yet presented.

The 'interpolated testing' study he describes: students quizzed partway through a three-part seminar not only recalled the already-covered material better than a restudy control group, but also performed better on a final test of the later segment 3 material - which both groups experienced identically.
The quizzed group also self-reported better attention and less mind-wandering during the later, unquizzed segment, evidence that test expectancy actively primes attention forward, not just backward.

Hobbiss's practical formula: a CFU only delivers all three benefits if it is signposted/cued to students in advance of the information being presented, and requires the active use of information from memory (not passive recognition).

His candid closing caveat: cueing attention precisely, without the cue itself becoming a source of distraction, 'is not easy' - the art of teaching is needed to apply the research evidence well in a real classroom.
quotes: These pieces usually focus on CFU as a tool of assessment for learning. They stress the value of CFU in helping teachers to diagnose the level of understanding at a whole class level.
This therefore illustrates the second benefit of a good CFU; providing retrieval opportunities which improve learning or prior material.
BUT... something unusual also happens. The 'test' group also do better in the final test on content from segment 3. This is odd, because both groups have an identical experience during segment 3.
In other words, the third benefit of a good CFU is that it works forwards into the future, aiding new learning which takes place after the check.
The art of teaching is needed to create the conditions in which the science of teaching can be usefully deployed.
Cueing attention, in both space and time, has the potentially to be a powerful educational lever. It's not easy though.
